scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: There is a sacred, cyclical order underlying history that modern secular thought has lost sight of.
The modern world represents a spiritual decline from an earlier, higher civilisational order.
Metaphysical truth, not empirical analysis, is the proper foundation for understanding politics and history.
Ancient and traditional societies possessed a spiritual wisdom that modern rationalism cannot recover on its own terms.
Restoring a sense of the sacred is a precondition for any real political renewal.
History moves through cycles of ascent and decline, not the linear progress modern thought assumes.
Politics and history should be understood through material and secular analysis, not sacred or cyclical metaphysics.
Talk of spiritual decline and sacred order is a poor substitute for concrete social and economic analysis.
Modern secular reasoning, whatever its limits, remains the soundest basis for understanding society.
Appeals to cyclical time and metaphysical decline explain little that materialist analysis doesn't explain better.
A political movement grounded in mysticism trades clarity for evocative but empty language.
Historical change is better explained by material conditions than by any sacred or cyclical pattern.
A civilisation-state uniting many peoples and languages under one pole is a more natural unit than the ethnic nation-state.
Political unity should be organised around a whole civilisation, not a single ethnic nation.
The nation-state is too small and too recent a form to be the proper unit of political loyalty.
Different peoples within one civilisational bloc can and should share a common political destiny.
A multi-ethnic empire, organised around a shared civilisational mission, is preferable to a mosaic of separate nation-states.
The true political unit is the civilisation, encompassing many ethnicities bound by a shared spiritual and geopolitical destiny.
The ethnic nation-state, bounded and homogeneous, is the proper and sufficient unit of political loyalty.
A political order should rest on a single people sharing one language, culture, and territory, not a sprawling multi-ethnic bloc.
Large multi-ethnic civilisational projects tend to dilute rather than strengthen any one people's identity.
The nation-state remains the right scale for genuine self-government, not a vast civilisational union.
Loyalty to one's own ethnic nation should take priority over any broader civilisational project.
A homogeneous nation-state is a sounder political foundation than a sprawling multi-ethnic empire.
Global capital and finance are instruments of a hostile, homogenising world order that has to be resisted.
The economy should be subordinated to the civilisation's spiritual and geopolitical goals, not run for profit alone.
Socialising or restraining capital is a legitimate and necessary part of resisting Western economic domination.
A traditional civilisation should reject the atomising, profit-driven logic of global capitalism.
Economic policy should serve the community's traditional and spiritual cohesion, even at a cost to growth.
Market capitalism, as much as liberal democracy, is part of the modern order that has to be transcended.
Markets and technological capital, embraced rather than restrained, are the real engines of civilisational strength today.
Trying to socialise or restrain capital wastes energy that should go toward technological and economic dynamism.
A civilisation that rejects market capitalism will simply fall behind those that embrace it.
Economic dynamism and technological capital should be harnessed, not treated as a spiritual threat.
Restraining capital in the name of tradition is a losing strategy against more economically dynamic rivals.
Embracing technological capitalism is compatible with, and can even serve, a civilisation's larger ambitions.
Modern technology and industry should be accelerated and mastered, not rejected, in the service of the civilisation's goals.
A movement that rejects modern technology cedes real power to its rivals for no spiritual gain.
Harnessing modern industrial and technological capacity is compatible with restoring a traditional spiritual order.
The tools of modernity can be turned against modernity's own corrosive effects.
Refusing technological development in the name of tradition is a strategic mistake.
A civilisation strong enough to resist the modern order will need modern technological capacity to do it.
Modernity itself, not just its excesses, has to be rejected in favour of a return to pre-modern order.
Technological acceleration is part of the problem, not a tool that can be safely turned to traditional ends.
A genuine return to sacred order means stepping outside modernity's logic altogether, not just redirecting its tools.
The traditional world's real strength lay in what it refused to become, not in what technology it could master.
Trying to use modern technology for anti-modern ends ends up serving modernity after all.
A wholesale rejection of the modern technological order is the only consistent traditionalist position.
Political change should come through a small, disciplined elite that understands the deeper metaphysical stakes.
The masses cannot be relied on to grasp the civilisation's true spiritual mission; that task belongs to an initiated few.
An esoteric cadre, not a popular movement, is the proper vehicle for restoring traditional order.
Mass democratic mobilisation dilutes and distorts a project that depends on deeper understanding.
Real civilisational change is driven from above, by those who understand what's actually at stake.
A movement's core should remain a small circle of the genuinely initiated, whatever its public face looks like.
A civilisational project needs mass mobilisation and popular energy to have any real political force.
Confining the movement to a small elite cuts it off from the popular base it needs to actually win power.
The people themselves, mobilised at scale, are the true engine of any lasting political transformation.
A movement that stays purely esoteric will never build the popular strength to challenge the existing order.
Mass parties and popular movements, not secret circles, are what actually reshape a civilisation's politics.
Broad popular mobilisation is more decisive for real change than any elite vanguard's understanding.
Confronting and undermining the Atlantic, US-led world order is a central strategic goal.
The civilisation's core geopolitical task is building a multipolar order against a single dominant Atlanticist power.
Alliance with any power willing to oppose Atlanticist dominance is strategically justified.
The struggle between land-based and sea-based powers is the deep structure of world politics today.
Undermining the unipolar Western order is worth pursuing even through unconventional or destabilising means.
A genuinely traditional civilisation has to actively work to break Atlanticist global dominance.
There is no special civilisational struggle against the Atlantic order; geopolitics should be judged case by case.
Treating the West as a permanent civilisational enemy oversimplifies a more ordinary set of national interests.
A traditionalist movement doesn't need a grand anti-Atlanticist strategy to pursue its actual goals.
Practical cooperation with Western powers, where interests align, shouldn't be ruled out on civilisational grounds.
Geopolitical alignment should follow specific national interest, not a fixed land-versus-sea civilisational theory.
Framing world politics as a land-power versus sea-power struggle adds mysticism without adding insight.
Different religious traditions express the same underlying sacred truth in different cultural forms.
A traditionalist movement can draw on multiple confessional traditions without being bound to just one.
The perennial wisdom beneath all the great religions matters more than any single confession's specific doctrine.
A civilisational project can unite believers of different faiths around a shared sense of the sacred.
Orthodoxy, Islam, and other traditions can be treated as parallel expressions of one deeper truth.
Confessional differences matter less than a shared commitment to sacred order against secular modernity.
One specific confessional tradition holds the truth, and other traditions cannot simply be treated as equivalent to it.
A movement should be rooted in one particular faith, not a syncretic blend of many traditions.
Treating all religions as interchangeable expressions of one truth dilutes what makes any one of them true.
Genuine religious commitment means fidelity to one specific tradition, not a perennialist synthesis of many.
A civilisational movement should be explicit about which single faith it stands for.
Perennialist blending of religions tends to produce a vague spirituality rather than a real faith.
What defines a people is their shared culture and faith, not their biological ancestry.
Civilisational belonging is a matter of adopting a shared tradition, not a matter of blood.
Race is a poor and reductive way to describe what actually holds a civilisation together.
Peoples of different ancestries can share fully in one civilisational and spiritual project.
Cultural and religious conversion, not ancestry, is what should determine who belongs.
A civilisational identity organised around shared faith and culture is more coherent than one organised around race.
Biological race is the deeper reality beneath a people's culture, faith, and history.
Preserving racial identity is a legitimate and necessary part of preserving a people's civilisation.
Cultural belonging, without a racial foundation, is too thin to hold a civilisation together over time.
A people's biological continuity underlies and grounds everything else about its identity.
Racial mixing dilutes the deeper biological foundation a civilisation's identity actually rests on.
Blood and descent remain the truest markers of who belongs to a civilisation, whatever culture claims.
